I’m constantly going over old mistakes—things like misshelving books years ago or snapping at a coworker once—and telling myself I’m useless, that it’s no wonder I’m still single. Every small misstep feels like proof that I’m fundamentally flawed.

Sometimes I’ll have a day or two where I feel a bit more energetic or talkative, maybe stay up late reorganizing my apartment, but it never gets to the point where I’m out of control or doing anything reckless, and it never lasts very long. I’ve felt like this low, heavy cloud has been over me for a little over three years now, pretty much nonstop. I wake up already feeling sad and worn out, and it doesn’t really lift during the day. I tear up embarrassingly easily—commercials, small frustrations—sometimes I’m at my desk trying to fix some ancient COBOL code and I have to turn away so nobody sees my eyes watering.  

I’m constantly second‑guessing myself. Even things I’ve done for decades at work, I’ll sit there worrying, “Did I screw that up? Did I miss something in the job control?” I ask coworkers to double‑check simple stuff because I just don’t trust my own judgment anymore.  

My memory feels off too. I misplace my tools, forget where I put printouts, walk into a room and can’t remember what I came for. It’s not like I’m confused, but my focus is so poor it feels like my brain’s “slipping.”  

Every once in a while I’ll get a couple of days where I sleep less and feel a bit more driven—clean the apartment, refactor old scripts—but it never gets extreme, and people don’t say I’m acting different or wired.
